paras: The lynching of James B. Brown took place in early January 1881 at Lake Providence, East Carroll Parish, Louisiana, when a group of men broke open the parish jail, took out Brown, who was held on a charge of murdering the town's city marshal, and hanged him. A coroner's jury was later reported to believe he had been shot and beaten to death before he reached the scaffold. The killing was carried by wire across the country, and several north Louisiana weeklies condemned it as the murder of a prisoner in the hands of the law.

Brown was described as an Illinois flatboatman who had arrived at Lake Providence with eleven or twelve others in January 1880. According to the New Orleans Picayune, reprinted in the Lake Charles Echo, the party became "boisterous and quarrelsome from drinking too freely," and when City Marshal Bernard McGuire warned Brown, its ringleader, that he would be arrested, Brown drew a revolver and shot him dead. The Picayune added that McGuire's Irish friends later fired on the other flatboatmen in their place of confinement, wounding three, and that reports of eighteen or nineteen deaths had been false.
Brown escaped, was recognized in Mississippi about six months later, and was jailed at Lake Providence to await trial; no report states his race.

The lynching took place at night while Sheriff Powell and his deputies were in New Orleans, where Powell was to answer a charge of murdering Dr. Jones, editor of the Republican. A party of armed men broke open the jail and took Brown out. Local and Louisiana reports placed the hanging on the scaffold in the court-house square, while a Memphis dispatch said a lamppost and a reprinted news digest said a tree.

The lynchers were reported as "persons unknown," but the Picayune said it was supposed that friends of McGuire had done it. The Memphis dispatch likewise said the marshal's friends "were tired of the tardiness of justice."

A coroner's jury was investigating by the time the first dispatch was sent. Later in the month the Morehouse Clarion reported that the inquest jury thought Brown had been "shot and beaten to death before he reached the scaffold," covered with blood and mutilated. The Memphis dispatch stated that no arrests had been made, and no report of an arrest, indictment or trial of the lynchers appears in the coverage. The Richland Beacon called on "all good citizens of East Carroll" to bring the perpetrators to punishment.

Wire versions ran on January 12 in the New-York Tribune under the headline "Lynch Law in Louisiana," the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, the Wilmington Daily Republican and the Savannah Morning News. A longer news-digest paragraph that named Brown an Illinois flatboatman and retold the marshal's killing appeared in weeklies in Mississippi, Tennessee, Arkansas, Missouri and Louisiana between January 15 and 29. These national items stated Brown's guilt as fact, saying he "murdered" the marshal or calling him "the murderer."

Louisiana weeklies were sharper: the Monroe Bulletin, quoted in the Morehouse Clarion, said Lake Providence "owes it to itself to ferret out the murderers" and called lynching a powerless prisoner "brutal and cowardly." In February the Richland Beacon reprinted and endorsed a Madison Journal editorial that cited Brown's case, called lynching "murder nevertheless," and warned that it would keep immigrants away and cost a parish "more than the loss of a crop."

Reports disagreed on the night of the lynching. A dispatch dated Lake Providence, January 7, said Brown was taken out "last night," and the Claiborne Guardian of January 19 said "a week ago last Thursday night," both pointing to Thursday, January 6; as the earliest and nearest report, the dated dispatch is the strongest evidence. The Picayune gave Friday evening and the news digest the night of the 7th, while the Monroe Bulletin and the Richland Beacon gave the night of the 4th. The Savannah Morning News said Saturday night, the Wilmington Daily Republican Sunday night, and the Memphis dispatch of January 11 "night before last."
The Picayune also dated the marshal's killing to January 1881, which conflicts with its own account and with other reports placing it in January 1880.

framing.detail: National dailies ran the Memphis wire as 'Lynch Law in Louisiana' or as a one-sentence brief stating that Brown 'murdered' the marshal.
A news-digest paragraph carried in several weeklies retold the marshal's killing at length, calling Brown 'the murderer' and the 'ringleader'.

The Monroe Bulletin (via the Morehouse Clarion) called lynching a powerless prisoner 'brutal and cowardly'; the Richland Beacon demanded punishment and later endorsed a Madison Journal editorial calling lynching murder.
